chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Harun ibn Muslim, from Ibn Sadan, from Mas'adah ibn Sadah, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father (peace be upon him), who said:

Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no bequest for an heir, nor is there a confession of a debt [for an heir] — meaning: if the sick person confesses to one of the heirs that he has a debt to him, it is not valid for him.'.

Therefore, this report came to the place of precaution (taqiyyah), because it includes that there is no bequest for an heir, nor a confession of a debt for him. And we have clarified that his confession to the heirs is valid, and we will clarify later, if God Almighty wills, that he has the right to bequeath to his heirs. So after that, nothing remains but to interpret the narration according to what we said. It is also possible that the meaning is: no confession of a debt in what exceeds one-third, if he is suspected (of bias), because we have clarified that we do not validate the confession if the confessor is not trustworthy, except in what is less than one-third.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a dying person confessing a debt to one of their heirs?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq’s report by reconciling the general prohibition of bequests to heirs with the validity of debt confessions, attributing the restriction to *taqiyyah* (precaution) or suspicion of self-dealing. He clarifies that while an heir can acknowledge a debt, it is limited to one-third of the estate if the heir is deemed 'suspected' (*muttaham*), ensuring fairness among all beneficiaries. This reflects the Shia juristic approach of balancing textual literalism with practical equity in inheritance law.
